amendments.rule: **A subordinating conjunction the ASV supplies for a clause whose Hebrew writes none is `added`.** Casuistic law opens its protasis with אִם, with כִּי, or with a waw, and where one of these stands in the clause it takes the ASV's *if*, *when* or *that* by rules 14 and 30: the corpus aligns a waw to *if* and to *when*, and כִּי takes whichever of them the ASV has written for it. But the ASV also writes such a word for a clause that has no conjunction in it at all — *and, behold,* ***if*** *the plague be spread* for וְהִנֵּה פָּשָׂה הַנֶּגַע, and the italic ***yet*** of *he is bald,* ***yet*** *is he clean* for קֵרֵחַ הוּא טָהוֹר הוּא — and there no morpheme licenses it: it is its own `added` unit under rule 30. Do not fold it into the waw that opens the clause, into הִנֵּה, or into the verb, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and* and rule 51 about a supplied *also* — the word is written beside those renderings rather than inside one of them, and the waw and הִנֵּה already have the *and* and the *behold* the ASV wrote for them. Count the clause's conjunctions against the ASV's subordinators, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s, and mark whichever side is in surplus. **But a coordinator and a subordinator the ASV writes together for one connective morpheme are one rendering of that morpheme, and neither word is a surplus.** Where the ASV recasts that connective's own clause as a subordinate one and writes the pair at that clause's left edge — *And when I looked* for וָאֶרְאֶה, *And when I see the blood* for וְרָאִיתִי, and likewise *and that* and *so that* — both English words belong to that connective's single unit, and the count above marks nothing `added` unless no conjunction stands in the clause at all. Contiguity is the test, exactly as in rule 30: what makes the Leviticus *if* above a surplus is that הִנֵּה's *behold* stands between it and the waw's *and*, so the *if* is written beside those renderings rather than as part of one connective. **Read the connective that is there and not its lemma.** A disjunctive אוֹ whose clause the ASV recasts the same way takes the pair on the same terms as a waw — `אוֹ־עָבַר עָלָיו רוּחַ־קִנְאָה` → ***or if*** *the spirit of jealousy come upon him* is one unit on the אוֹ, headed on *or* — since what licenses the pair is the one connective the ASV has rendered by it and not the lemma, exactly as rule 14 reads אוֹ and a waw alike where one connective is written in two English words. But where a morpheme of its own stands in the clause for the subordinator, that morpheme takes it and there is no pair to place: `אוֹ אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר תַּעֲבֹר עָלָיו` → *or* ***when*** *the spirit of jealousy cometh upon a man* gives *or* to the אוֹ and *when* to the אֲשֶׁר, a present morpheme taking its English before a fused reading does. Head such a unit on the coordinator, which is what the connective itself is; the corpus aligns a waw to *and when* in twenty-seven units, to *so that* in thirty-eight and to *and that* in eight, heading eleven of the *and when* units on *when* instead, so name that competing reading in the note under rule 8. **But read that head directive by what the written connective is, and not by which English word stands first.** What it says is that the head goes on the word the connective itself is, and the connective of every case above is a coordinator. Where instead the morpheme the pair renders is itself a subordinator — a כִּי or an אִם the ASV answers with *for though*, *and though*, *and if* or *and when* — the subordinating word is what realizes that morpheme's own lexeme and the coordinator standing beside it realizes nothing of it, so head there, exactly as rule 24 puts a target head on the token most directly realizing the source head's lexeme and rule 23 heads a fused unit on the morpheme carrying the content. `כִּי יַעַר הוּא` → ***for though*** *it is a forest* and `כִּי חָזָק הוּא` → ***and though*** *they are strong* both head on *though*, and the bare `כִּי` → *though* the ASV writes beside them in that verse is what identifies the word. Read the Hebrew morpheme rather than the English order, since the coordinator stands first in either case and one verse may write both pairs, as JOS.17.18 does; where the pair's two words both render senses the connective itself carries, choose the one subordinating the clause the unit heads and name the other in the note under rule 8. **And a subordinator the ASV writes a second time for a clause coordinated under one the Hebrew has already written is that morpheme's own repeated realization, not a surplus.** Where a single אֲשֶׁר or כִּי governs coordinated clauses and the ASV rewrites its *that* at the head of a later one, every occurrence belongs to that morpheme's one possibly discontinuous unit under rule 25, exactly as a distributed `מִן` takes both of its *from*s there and a paraphrased suffix takes both of its pronouns under rule 18; head on the first, and mark nothing `added`. `לְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יִגְבְּהוּ ... וְלֹא־יִתְּנוּ ... וְלֹא־יַעַמְדוּ` → *to the end* ***that*** *none ... exalt themselves ..., neither set their top ..., nor* ***that*** *their mighty ones stand up* gives both *that*s to the one אֲשֶׁר, the waws keeping only the *neither* and *nor* they are fused into. So read whether the later clause is coordinated under an earlier subordinator's scope before counting: what the count governs is a subordinator standing over a clause no written subordinator reaches, as the Leviticus protasis above has no conjunction in it at all. **And read that scope before reading a coordinator and a subordinator as a pair.** Where a written subordinator governs coordinated clauses and the ASV opens a later one with both a connective for its waw and a rewritten copy of that subordinator, the two English words answer to two morphemes and not to one: the waw takes only the coordinator written for it, and the subordinator's second occurrence joins the written אִם, כִּי, אֲשֶׁר or לְמַעַן as that morpheme's discontinuous unit, headed on the first. `וְאִם־לֹא קָרוֹב אָחִיךָ אֵלֶיךָ וְלֹא יְדַעְתּוֹ` → *And* ***if*** *thy brother be not nigh unto thee,* ***or if*** *thou know him not* gives *or* to the second waw and both *if*s to the one אִם, which opens the protasis and governs both of its members, exactly as לְמַעַן takes both *that*s of `לְמַעַן יִיטַב לָךְ וְהַאֲרַכְתָּ יָמִים` → *that it may be well with thee, and* ***that*** *thou mayest prolong thy days* while its waw keeps only the *and*. This is the carve-out the preceding paragraph makes for a morpheme standing in the clause itself, read for a subordinator whose scope reaches that clause from an earlier member of the coordination: a present morpheme takes its English before a fused reading does, whichever member of the coordination it stands in, and a waw already holding a connective of its own is not a home for a second word, as rule 51 says. So ask whether the subordinator the ASV has written a second time is one the Hebrew has already written for that same coordination before giving the pair to the connective. What the pair sentence governs is a clause no written subordinator reaches, which is what `וָאֶרְאֶה` → *And when I looked* is, and reading the two shapes apart is a matter of the Hebrew's scope rather than of which English words stand side by side. **And a word that belongs to a formula's own fixed English rendering is not a subordinator supplied for the clause: it belongs to the morpheme the formula rests on.** The oath חַי־אָנִי is written *As I live*, and the *As* is what English spends on the adverbial force of that predicate adjective, exactly as rule 20 takes the copula from the construction and rule 30 takes the pronouns of נָא's *I beseech thee* from the particle's one idiomatic rendering: the adjective takes *As … live* in one unit, discontinuous around the pronoun under rule 25 and headed on *live*, while an explicit אָנִי or אֲנִי takes only its own *I*. The corpus reads the formula this way in six chapters and never marks the *As* `added`. So before counting an English subordinator as a surplus, read whether it is one the formula always writes; the count above governs a word the ASV has supplied for the clause, not a word the formula's rendering contains.
amendments.why: Rule 55's head directive — 'Head such a unit on the coordinator, which is what the connective itself is' — was written from waw examples, where the two halves of the sentence agree. JOS.17.18 writes the pair twice for a `כִּי`, where they come apart: the coordinator is an English *for* or *and* that realizes nothing of a subordinating connective, so the literal directive would put a `כִּי` head on *and*, against rule 24's requirement that the target head realize the source head's lexeme. The verse pass followed the directive in one unit and the rationale in the other, and headed the same construction two ways. The amendment keeps the rule's stated reason and makes the literal wording follow it, citing rules 23 and 24, and it takes nothing away: the waw cases and their corpus counts, including the eleven *and when* units headed on *when*, stand as before.

conventions: A `כִּי` the ASV renders by a coordinator plus a subordinator — *for though*, *and though* — is one rule 55 unit headed on the subordinating word, not on the coordinator. Rule 55's 'head on the coordinator' is written for a waw, whose own nature is coordinating; a `כִּי` is a subordinator, and JOS.17.18 writes a bare `כִּי` -> *though* beside the two pairs, which identifies the word realizing its lexeme.

Possessive `לְ` divides by what the source writes, and the chapter writes all three shapes. A written `הָיָה` takes the *had*, *shall have* or *shall be* itself and leaves its lamed `unrepresented` (vv. 1, 3, 11, 17, 18); a verbless possessive clause puts the *hast* or *have* on the preposition, `בְּ` as readily as `לְ` (vv. 16, 17, 18); and where the ASV writes the relation inside an English genitive and spends no word on the preposition, the lamed fuses with the following name under rule 49's closing paragraph and the construction's copula joins that unit (v. 10, *was Ephraim's*, *was Manasseh's*). A suffix rendered by a bare possessive — v. 18's *thine* — is not such a genitive, since that is the word a bare suffix takes in any case, so the lamed is `unrepresented` there.

Supplied English subjects: *this* in v. 1 is the subject pronoun of the written wayyiqtol under rule 17, while the two *it*s of v. 10 stand in verbless clauses where no morpheme can carry them and are `added` under rule 20's impersonal-*it* sentence. What decides it is whether a verb morpheme stands in the clause. A supplied lexical subject nominal is `added` either way — *the lot* (v. 2), *the inhabitants of* (v. 12).

The chapter's two *even*s are rule 16's own two cases. *even to Ephraim* (v. 17) is the expanded rendering of the `לְ` standing beside it, headed on *to*; *even the three heights* (v. 11) stands before a bare nominal with no marker and no preposition, and the verse's single object marker stands on `אֶת־יֹשְׁבֵי דֹאר`, so it is `added` and is not reached across the clause for.

JOS.17.18 writes the pair twice for a `כִּי`, where they come apart: the coordinator is an English *for* or *and* that realizes nothing of a subordinating connective, so the literal directive would put a `כִּי` head on *and*, against rule 24's requirement that the target head realize the source head's lexeme. The verse pass followed the directive in one unit and the rationale in the other, and headed the same construction two ways. The amendment keeps the rule's stated reason and makes the literal wording follow it, citing rules 23 and 24, and it takes nothing away: the waw cases and their corpus counts, including the eleven *and when* units headed on *when*, stand as before.

report: Read all 43 candidate groups and the whole dump end to end, since the table is blind to `added` units and this chapter has eight of them.

One real split, inside JOS.17.18: the two `כִּי` units the ASV renders by a coordinator plus *though* — s006 -> *for though*, s028 -> *and though* — are the same rule 55 construction but were headed differently (s006 on *for*, s028 on *though*), with the two unit notes giving contradictory rationales. Standardized on *though*, the word realizing this subordinating connective's own lexeme, as the bare `כִּי` -> *though* of *though they have chariots* in the same verse shows. Rule 55's 'head on the coordinator' is written for a waw, whose own nature is coordinating; heading a `כִּי` on an English *and* would put the head on a word that realizes nothing of it, against rule 24. Only that head moved — no edge changed.

Possessive `לְ` looked like a three-way split and is not. With a written `הָיָה` the verb takes the *had* / *shall have* / *shall be* and the lamed is unrepresented (vv. 1, 3, 11, 17, 18); in a verbless clause the preposition itself carries the *hast* / *have* (vv. 16, 17, 18); and where the ASV writes the relation inside an English genitive with no preposition of its own, the lamed fuses with the name under rule 49's closing paragraph (v. 10, *Ephraim's*, *Manasseh's*). Each difference is licensed by what the source writes.

Supplied English subjects divide by the source too: *this* in v. 1 is the subject pronoun of a written wayyiqtol (rule 17), the two *it*s of v. 10 stand in verbless clauses with no morpheme to carry them and are `added` (rule 20), and the supplied lexical nominals *the lot* (v. 2) and *the inhabitants of* (v. 12) are `added` whether or not a verb stands.

The two *even*s are rule 16's own distinction, not a split: v. 17's *even to Ephraim* has a `לְ` standing beside it and is that preposition's expanded rendering, while v. 11's *even the three heights* stands before a bare nominal and the verse's one object marker stands on `אֶת־יֹשְׁבֵי דֹאר`, so it is `added`.

Phrasal particles were checked against rule 44's subtraction and are consistent: *down* joins `יָרַד` and `בָּרָא`, *out* joins `יָרַשׁ`, *up* joins `עָלָה`, while v. 7's *along* is `added` because *went* alone already writes `הָלַךְ`.

The v. 5 large-source unit `לְבַד ... מִן` -> *besides* was re-checked: the morphemes are contiguous, one English word carries the separation and the ablative alike, and the corpus fuses `מִלְּבַד` to *besides* at 1KI.10.13. Left as aligned.

BSB: 26 disagreements, none a genuine error. The R x 14 and Td x 8 blocks are the documented convention differences (rules 27, 29, 40), the v. 10 paragogic nun is rule 32, the v. 3 `וֹ` is a suffix the ASV leaves unrendered beside the name that realizes the subject (rule 22), the v. 5 `לַ` is silenced by *beyond* (rule 40), and the v. 18 `וּ` opens an apodosis for which the ASV writes no connective (rule 14).
